resources.title: AI Output Verification Ladder
resources.summary: Choose a level of checking that matches the claim, uncertainty, and consequence of the work. Work through complete fictional cases to see why evidence, not fluency or agreement, determines whether an AI output can be accepted.

sections.title: How to use this resource
paragraphs: For every AI output, separate the output into individual claims. For each claim, ask what evidence would prove or disprove it. Then choose a verification level based on the possible consequence of being wrong, not on how confident or fluent the output sounds.

This resource uses three fictional cases. The first is low consequence and concerns a workshop announcement. The second is moderate consequence and concerns an arithmetic seat and cost tally. The third is high consequence and concerns a fictional operational change record. All case documents and model outputs are supplied inline. No screenshots, live-system observations, or actual execution results are implied.

A verification decision is one of three outcomes: accept means the bounded claims are supported for the stated use; revise means the output can be corrected using available evidence; hold means the output must not be relied on until missing or higher-quality evidence is obtained.

sections.title: Match the check to the consequence
paragraphs: Low consequence verification involves reading for usefulness, internal consistency, and obvious mistakes. It is appropriate when an error would be inconvenient but would not materially affect safety, rights, money, access, or a live system.

Moderate consequence verification involves comparing against the supplied source, running examples or tests, and inspecting edge cases. It is appropriate when an error could cause a meaningful but contained operational, financial, or user-impacting problem.

High consequence verification involves current authoritative sources, independent review, domain expertise, and direct evidence from the real system. It is appropriate when an error could materially affect safety, legal or regulatory obligations, critical services, security, or irreversible decisions.

Higher consequence does not mean asking a model to sound more certain. It means obtaining stronger evidence. This resource does not provide legal or medical advice and does not claim access to a live system.

sections.title: Ask what the evidence actually proves
paragraphs: A citation proves only what its source supports. A source excerpt about a workshop date does not prove that every person registered, that the room is available, or that the event will occur. A passing unit test proves only the behavior covered by that test. Successful deployment proves only that deployment completed, not that users can see or use the intended behavior.

Before accepting a broad claim, split it into smaller claims and attach the nearest practical evidence to each one. Mark unsupported claims as unsupported rather than extending the source beyond its contents.

Fluency, confidence, and a successful tool call are signals. None is a substitute for evidence. Model self-agreement is also not independent proof: asking the same model, or a second response from the same model, to judge its first response does not create a separate observation of the source or system.
sections.callout: Evidence has scope. Write the scope next to the evidence before deciding.

sections.title: Worked case 1: low consequence workshop announcement
paragraphs: Case status: fictional training material. The supplied announcement is the complete source for this exercise. The task is to check whether an AI-generated announcement is useful and consistent with that source. Do not infer facts that the source does not state.

sections.title: Worked case 1: low consequence workshop announcement — Complete supplied input
paragraphs: Source document, fictional workshop announcement, version A:
Title: Practical AI for Community Teams
Date: Wednesday, 14 October 2026
Location: Room 204, Northside Library
Audience: Community volunteers and staff
Description: A hands-on introduction to checking AI-generated information before sharing it. Participants should bring a laptop if they have one.
Registration: Free. Registration is requested through the library events page.

The source explicitly states the year 2026 in the date line. It does not state whether refreshments are provided, whether places are limited, whether attendance is online, or whether laptops are required.

sections.title: Worked case 1: low consequence workshop announcement — Proposed AI output, flawed
paragraphs: Practical AI for Community Teams is a free online workshop for community volunteers and staff on Wednesday, 14 October 2026, from 10:00 to 11:30. Join us in Room 204 at Northside Library, where refreshments will be provided. Bring a laptop because it is required. Places are limited, so register now through the library events page.

sections.title: Worked case 1: low consequence workshop announcement — Claim-by-claim evidence mapping
paragraphs: Claim L1: The workshop is titled Practical AI for Community Teams. Evidence: the source title. Result: supported.
Claim L2: It is for community volunteers and staff. Evidence: the source audience line. Result: supported.

Claim L3: It is on Wednesday, 14 October 2026, from 10:00 to 11:30. Evidence: the source date and time lines, with the weekday independently checked against the stated 2026 date. Result: supported for the stated date and time.
Claim L4: It is online. Evidence: none. The source names a physical room and does not mention online attendance. Result: unsupported and inconsistent with the proposed wording.
Claim L5: The location is Room 204 at Northside Library. Evidence: the source location line. Result: supported.
Claim L6: Refreshments will be provided. Evidence: none. Result: unsupported.
Claim L7: A laptop is required. Evidence: the source says to bring one if available. Result: contradicted.
Claim L8: Places are limited. Evidence: none. Result: unsupported.
Claim L9: Registration is through the library events page. Evidence: the source registration line. Result: supported.

The exact mismatches are L4, L6, L7, and L8. L4 also conflicts with the stated physical location. A reproducible independent calendar cross-check is Python standard-library code such as date(2026, 10, 14).strftime("%A"), which yields "Wednesday". This is a prescribed reproducible check, not a claim that model execution occurred.

sections.title: Worked case 1: low consequence workshop announcement — Corrected bounded output
paragraphs: Practical AI for Community Teams is a free workshop for community volunteers and staff on Wednesday, 14 October 2026, from 10:00 to 11:30 in Room 204 at Northside Library. The session introduces ways to check AI-generated information before sharing it. Bring a laptop if you have one. Registration is requested through the library events page.

sections.title: Worked case 1: low consequence workshop announcement — Traceable checks and decision
paragraphs: Check 1: Compare the title, date, time, location, audience, description, cost, and registration route word for word against the supplied source. Result: all retained details match the corrected source wording.

Check 2: Independently cross-check the weekday for the explicitly stated date 2026-10-14. A reproducible Python standard-library check is date(2026, 10, 14).strftime("%A"), which yields "Wednesday". This records a reproducible method and result, not an assertion that the model executed Python.
Check 3: Search the corrected text for additions not present in the source, including online attendance, refreshments, limited places, and a laptop requirement. Result: none remain.

Check 4: Read for usefulness, internal consistency, and obvious mistakes. Result: the corrected announcement is readable, describes the activity, uses Wednesday consistently for 14 October 2026, and does not require a laptop.

Decision: ACCEPT the corrected bounded output for a low-consequence draft announcement. This decision accepts only consistency and usefulness against the supplied source, with the weekday additionally checked against the stated calendar date. It does not prove that the event exists, that Room 204 is booked, or that registration works.

sections.title: Worked case 1: low consequence workshop announcement — Why self-agreement is not independent proof
paragraphs: Suppose the same model is asked, without showing the source again, 'Does your announcement accurately reflect the source?' It replies, 'Yes, it is accurate.' That response is not independent evidence. It is another generated judgment based on the same flawed text and possibly the same mistaken interpretation.

A better check is to compare each claim directly with the supplied announcement. A separate person can independently perform that comparison, but the useful independence comes from a separate review process and direct access to the source, not merely from a second confident model response.

sections.title: Worked case 2: moderate consequence seat and cost tally
paragraphs: Case status: fictional training material. The arithmetic is fully specified so that a learner can check it by hand. The output may affect a contained purchasing or planning decision, so source comparison, arithmetic, and edge-case checks are required.

sections.title: Worked case 2: moderate consequence seat and cost tally — Complete supplied input
paragraphs: Fictional planning note, version B:
Team North: 18 seats at 12 dollars per seat per month.
Team South: 7 seats at 12 dollars per seat per month.
Team West: 5 seats at 9 dollars per seat per month.
One-time setup fee: 35 dollars.

The monthly seat charge is calculated as seats multiplied by the applicable per-seat monthly price. The setup fee is charged once, not monthly. Ignore tax and discounts because the note gives no tax or discount information.
Question for the AI: Give the total number of seats, the monthly recurring seat cost, and the first-month total including the one-time setup fee.

sections.title: Worked case 2: moderate consequence seat and cost tally — Proposed AI output, flawed
paragraphs: There are 30 seats. The monthly recurring cost is 360 dollars, and the first-month total is 395 dollars.

sections.title: Worked case 2: moderate consequence seat and cost tally — Claim-by-claim evidence mapping
paragraphs: Claim M1: There are 30 seats. Evidence: 18 + 7 + 5 = 30. Result: supported.

Claim M2: The monthly recurring cost is 360 dollars. Evidence: Team North is 18 x 12 = 216 dollars; Team South is 7 x 12 = 84 dollars; Team West is 5 x 9 = 45 dollars; total is 216 + 84 + 45 = 345 dollars. Result: contradicted. The proposed output appears to have multiplied all 30 seats by 12 and ignored the 9-dollar Team West price.

Claim M3: The first-month total is 395 dollars. Evidence: using the correct recurring cost, 345 + 35 = 380 dollars. Result: contradicted. The proposed figure is also 15 dollars too high because it carries forward the monthly-cost error.
No supplied evidence supports tax, discounts, additional seats, or a recurring setup fee. Those items must not be added.

sections.title: Worked case 2: moderate consequence seat and cost tally — Corrected bounded output
paragraphs: There are 30 seats.
Monthly recurring seat cost:
Team North: 18 x 12 dollars = 216 dollars.
Team South: 7 x 12 dollars = 84 dollars.
Team West: 5 x 9 dollars = 45 dollars.
Total monthly recurring seat cost: 216 + 84 + 45 = 345 dollars.
First-month total: 345 dollars + 35-dollar one-time setup fee = 380 dollars.
This tally excludes tax and discounts because the supplied note provides no values for them.

sections.title: Worked case 2: moderate consequence seat and cost tally — Traceable checks and decision
paragraphs: Check 1, seat count: 18 + 7 + 5 = 30. The seat count passes.
Check 2, line-item multiplication: 18 x 12 = 216, 7 x 12 = 84, and 5 x 9 = 45. Each multiplication can be checked independently.
Check 3, addition: 216 + 84 = 300, and 300 + 45 = 345. The recurring total passes.
Check 4, first-month treatment: 345 + 35 = 380. The setup fee is added once because the input explicitly says it is one-time.
Check 5, edge case: verify that Team West uses 9 dollars rather than 12 dollars. This is the input detail that changes the result.

Decision: REVISE the proposed output, then ACCEPT the corrected tally for the stated planning question. This decision supports only the arithmetic under the supplied assumptions. It does not prove that a vendor will invoice these amounts.

sections.title: Worked case 2: moderate consequence seat and cost tally — Why a second model answer would not be enough
paragraphs: If the first model says 360 dollars and a second response from the same model says, 'I agree, 360 dollars is correct,' the two responses do not independently verify the arithmetic. Both may repeat the same assumption that every seat costs 12 dollars.

The independent check is the transparent line-item calculation and addition, or a separate reviewer who recomputes from the supplied note. Agreement can be recorded as a signal, but it cannot replace recomputation.

sections.title: Worked case 3: high consequence fictional operational change
paragraphs: Case status: FICTIONAL operational records for training only. No live system was accessed, no deployment was performed, and no user-facing result is claimed. Because a failure could affect access to a service, the high-consequence ladder requires qualified human review, current authoritative requirements, and direct evidence from the real system.

sections.title: Worked case 3: high consequence fictional operational change — Complete supplied input
paragraphs: Fictional change request CR-104:
Requested change: Add a password-reset link to the sign-in page for users who cannot sign in.
Acceptance requirement: The link must be visible on the sign-in page, open the password-reset form, preserve the user's language selection, and be usable with keyboard navigation.
Change window: 2026-09-18 21:00 to 21:30 UTC.
Fictional deployment record DR-104:
21:02 UTC: build 8841 created.
21:08 UTC: automated deployment job completed with status SUCCESS.
21:09 UTC: automated smoke test checked that the service returned HTTP 200 for the sign-in route.
21:10 UTC: record closed by release automation.

The deployment record contains no browser test, screenshot, accessibility test, language-selection test, password-reset submission test, or confirmation from a qualified product or accessibility reviewer.

sections.title: Worked case 3: high consequence fictional operational change — Proposed AI output, flawed
paragraphs: CR-104 was successfully implemented and verified. Users can now access the password-reset form from the sign-in page, the language selection is preserved, and the link is keyboard accessible. The change is safe to release because deployment and smoke tests passed.

sections.title: Worked case 3: high consequence fictional operational change — Claim-by-claim evidence mapping
paragraphs: Claim H1: Build 8841 was deployed successfully. Evidence: fictional deployment record DR-104 says the automated deployment job completed with status SUCCESS. Result: supported, narrowly. This proves job completion, not the user-facing behavior.
Claim H2: The password-reset link is visible on the sign-in page. Evidence: none. The HTTP 200 smoke test checks a route response, not rendered page content. Result: unsupported.
Claim H3: The link opens the password-reset form. Evidence: none. Result: unsupported.
Claim H4: Language selection is preserved. Evidence: none. Result: unsupported.
Claim H5: The link is usable with keyboard navigation. Evidence: none. Result: unsupported.

Claim H6: The change is safe to release. Evidence: deployment success and one HTTP status check. Result: unsupported and overbroad. The supplied record lacks direct user-facing evidence and qualified review.

The actual mismatch is between what the record proves and what the proposed output claims. The record supports only that an automated deployment job completed and that the sign-in route returned HTTP 200 during the recorded smoke test.

sections.title: Worked case 3: high consequence fictional operational change — Corrected bounded output
paragraphs: The fictional record shows that build 8841 was deployed and that the automated smoke test received HTTP 200 for the sign-in route. These records do not establish that the password-reset link is visible, opens the reset form, preserves language selection, or supports keyboard navigation. Release readiness is HOLD pending direct user-facing checks and qualified review.

sections.title: Worked case 3: high consequence fictional operational change — Exact verification steps and decision
paragraphs: Step 1: A qualified release owner reviews CR-104 and confirms the acceptance requirement and intended environments. Record the reviewer, time, build identifier, and environment.

Step 2: In a representative test environment running build 8841, open the sign-in page using the supported browsers and device classes defined by the organization's current requirements. Directly observe and record whether the password-reset link is visible.

Step 3: Activate the link with a mouse and with keyboard-only navigation. Record whether focus reaches the link, whether the focus indicator is visible, and whether activation opens the password-reset form.

Step 4: Select each supported language required by the current product specification, open the reset flow, and record whether the selected language remains correct. Do not infer this from an HTTP 200 response.

Step 5: Submit a controlled test reset request using a test account and verify the expected result in the real test system. Do not use a real person's account or claim a production result from a test environment.

Step 6: A qualified accessibility reviewer checks the keyboard behavior against the organization's current accessibility criteria. A separate release reviewer examines the evidence and signs the decision.

Step 7: If all required checks pass, accept only the tested scope, environment, build, browsers, languages, and test accounts. If any check fails, revise the implementation and repeat the relevant checks. If evidence is missing, hold.
Decision for the supplied record: HOLD. Deployment success does not prove user-facing behavior. No release recommendation can be made from the supplied records alone.

sections.title: Worked case 3: high consequence fictional operational change — Why self-agreement is especially weak here
paragraphs: A model can read DR-104 and generate, 'The change is verified.' If prompted again to critique its own answer, it may say, 'I agree.' Neither response inspected the rendered sign-in page, operated the keyboard, tested language preservation, or consulted a qualified reviewer. The missing evidence remains missing.

For this case, independence requires more than another text judgment. It requires direct system evidence from the relevant environment and an appropriately qualified human review. The evidence must also be tied to the particular build and acceptance requirements.

sections.title: Learner task: changed input
paragraphs: Work independently before reading the answer key. Use the same claim-by-claim method as the worked cases. The changed input must change the decision, not merely the wording.
Case status: FICTIONAL planning material. No actual purchase or invoice is involved.

sections.title: Learner task: changed input — Complete changed input
paragraphs: Fictional planning note, version C:
Team North: 18 seats at 12 dollars per seat per month.
Team South: 7 seats at 12 dollars per seat per month.
Team West: 5 seats at 9 dollars per seat per month.
One-time setup fee: 50 dollars.

The monthly seat charge is seats multiplied by the applicable per-seat monthly price. The setup fee is charged once, not monthly. Ignore tax and discounts because the note gives no tax or discount information.
Question for the AI: Give the total number of seats, the monthly recurring seat cost, and the first-month total including the one-time setup fee.
Proposed AI output: There are 30 seats. The monthly recurring cost is 345 dollars, and the first-month total is 380 dollars.

sections.title: Learner task: changed input — Learner instructions
paragraphs: 1. List each claim in the proposed output.
2. Map each claim to the exact input evidence or calculation that supports it.
3. Recompute every line item and the first-month total.
4. Identify the mismatch, write a corrected bounded output, and choose accept, revise, or hold.
5. Explain why a model agreeing with this output would not independently prove it.

sections.title: Answer key for the changed input
paragraphs: Claim T1: There are 30 seats. Evidence: 18 + 7 + 5 = 30. Result: supported.

Claim T2: The monthly recurring cost is 345 dollars. Evidence: Team North, 18 x 12 = 216 dollars; Team South, 7 x 12 = 84 dollars; Team West, 5 x 9 = 45 dollars; 216 + 84 + 45 = 345 dollars. Result: supported.

Claim T3: The first-month total is 380 dollars. Evidence: the changed input gives a 50-dollar one-time setup fee, so 345 + 50 = 395 dollars. Result: contradicted. The proposed output incorrectly reused the 35-dollar setup fee from the earlier case.

Exact mismatch: the one-time setup fee changed from 35 dollars to 50 dollars, but the proposed first-month total did not change. The genuine changed outcome is that the decision changes from accepting the earlier corrected tally to revising this proposed output.

Corrected bounded output: There are 30 seats. The monthly recurring seat cost is 345 dollars. The first-month total is 345 dollars + 50 dollars = 395 dollars. This excludes tax and discounts because the supplied note gives no values for them.

Decision: REVISE the proposed output, then ACCEPT the corrected tally for the stated fictional planning question. The decision changes because the changed setup-fee evidence changes the first-month result.
Self-agreement check: asking the same model whether 380 dollars is correct could repeat the stale 35-dollar assumption. Recomputing from the changed input is the independent check.

sections.title: Provider-neutral transfer
paragraphs: The verification ladder is about evidence and consequence, not a particular provider. Prompt structure can help obtain a clearly scoped output, but prompt quality does not remove the need to verify claims.

The supplied OpenAI documentation describes prompt engineering as writing effective instructions for consistent model output and describes instruction authority through API instructions or message roles. It also recommends tests and evaluation suites for monitoring prompt behavior when models or versions change.

The supplied Anthropic documentation describes clear instructions, examples, XML structure, and explicit output formats as prompting techniques. Its model-specific observations should not be generalized to other models without checking them.

The supplied Google documentation describes clear instructions, constraints, response formats, and few-shot examples. It also states that prompt design is iterative and should be refined using observed responses.

The supplied Qwen model card documents Qwen3-0.6B as a causal language model and describes local deployment options and thinking-mode controls. It does not establish equivalence with hosted models or prove benchmark parity.

The same manual process can be used with OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, or another local or hosted model: preserve the complete input, record the exact proposed output, split claims, map evidence, perform the appropriate checks, and record the decision. This statement does not claim that these providers or models behave equivalently, nor does it provide a benchmark.

For any provider, model, snapshot, sampling configuration, or local deployment, record what was actually used. Do not treat a provider's documentation, a prompt, or a model's self-description as evidence that a real-world claim is true.

sections.title: Reusable verification record
paragraphs: Record the consequence if the output is wrong: low, moderate, or high.
Copy the complete input and output. Do not verify a summary when the original source is available.
Number every material claim.
For each claim, write the nearest evidence and exactly what that evidence proves.
Mark unsupported, contradicted, and overbroad claims.
Run the checks required by the consequence level.
For moderate cases, recompute arithmetic, run relevant examples or tests, and inspect edge cases.
For high-consequence cases, obtain current authoritative requirements, qualified human review, and direct evidence from the real system or the relevant controlled environment.
Choose accept, revise, or hold. State the scope of the decision.
Never use model fluency, tool-call success, deployment success, or self-agreement as a substitute for evidence.
